newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S., allies discuss North Korea contingency plans.
newsitem.headline: U.S., allies discuss North Korea contingency plans.

text.p: The United States, Japan and South Korea have been discussing contingency plans in the event of a "crisis" in famine-stricken communist North Korea, a senior Japanese government official said on Tuesday.
The official said reclusive North Korea, gripped by famine after two consecutive years of flooding, could run out of food within several months.
"Japan, the United States and South Korea have been exchanging information on the situation in North Korea," the official told Reuters in an interview.
"I would say we (the three countries) have been discussing contingency plans in the event of a crisis," he said on condition of anonymity. He declined to give details.
South Korea has already mapped out various crisis scenarios including a mass exodus of starving refugees, a military invasion and the collapse of Pyongyang's communist government.
The Japanese official said he ruled out the possibility of an uncontrolled outflow of refugees any time soon and the imminent collapse of the communist government.
"We don't see any possibility of a large-scale exodus of refugees at this stage," he said. "I also don't think the collapse of the government or the communist regime is imminent," he added.
Last month 17 North Koreans sought asylum in the capitalist South after fleeing through China to Hong Kong.

It was the biggest single flight from North Korea and set off alarm bells in Seoul that the North's deteriorating food and economic situation might soon become so dire that there would be a mass exodus.
South and North Korea remain technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce, not a peace pact.
The Japanese official painted a gloomy picture of the next few months for isolated North Korea whose economy has long been in dire straits.
"North Korea has already been in a considerable degree of (food) crisis," he said. "Food stocks would become extremely tight in March or April," he said.
"If North Korea failed in its efforts to secure enough food supplies from other countries, the food situation would reach a crisis point," he said.
"We believe North Korea does not have much food left now."

International relief agencies have reported that peasants in the North are scrounging for tree bark, grass and edible roots in their search for food because of the failure of two successive annual food crops due to floods.
Official figures show North Korea needs about 5.5 million tonnes of grain to feed its population but last year's harvest yielded just 3.5 million tonnes.
The Japanese official said there were no signs of any power strugle within the communist government.
"Although there are different opinions in the government, such as between the foreign ministry and military, the differences would not constitute any power struggle," he said.
